revisions.body: The opening gives the handoff a physical rhythm. Timaeus describes release from the difficult passage of his logos as rest after a long journey, then formally transfers the next logos to Critias according to their arrangements. One way to hear the metaphor is that Critias inherits a burden already in motion: the transition is not a new beginning, but a change of speaker carrying the discourse forward. That sense of inherited burden is an interpretation; the passage itself establishes the journey image and the formal transfer.

Critias turns an audience rule into a request for mercy. He says that mortal and human accounts receive exact scrutiny, then asks listeners to pardon any failure to render what is fitting. Ask yourself what this move changes: does it merely acknowledge the difficulty of representation, or does it invite the audience to judge the speech by the speaker’s stated limits before judging its likeness?

Socrates answers the request by making indulgence part of the conversation’s procedure: Hermocrates receives it in advance, so he can begin differently instead of repeating Critias’s prelude. Then Socrates shifts from courtesy to performance, warning Critias about the theatre’s enthusiastic reception of the previous poet. I hear a playful pressure here: the welcome lowers the cost of asking for pardon, while the comparison raises the standard the next speech must face.

At 109a, Critias turns geography into a promise about sequence: the many peoples will emerge as the account unrolls, but Athens and its opponents must come first, with Athens given priority within that pair. I read this as a deliberate narrowing of the story’s field: the wider war will initially be seen through Athens before the account opens outward.

The passage does not present the past as wholly erased. It preserves the rulers’ names, while their deeds have vanished and the surviving remnant knows only a few brief reports alongside those names. Read this as a portrait of selective transmission: a name can carry continuity without carrying a full account of conduct. The result is an inherited past with a clear limit—names remain, but the deeds they once identified cannot be recovered in full.

revisions.title: From preserved names to a civic design
revisions.body: This unit begins with Critias’s condition for ancient inquiry: myth-telling and investigation arrive with leisure once necessities are secured. It then turns from preserved names to a portrait of ancient Athens, where a distinct warrior class owns nothing privately, shares its possessions, and is said to practice the pursuits of yesterday’s hypothesized guardians.

The key distinction is between the condition Critias names and the evidence he offers. He says myth-telling and inquiry into antiquity arrive with leisure once necessities are secured; he then reports names preserved without their deeds, citing Solon’s account of what Egyptian priests recounted. One way to read this is as an attempt to reconstruct the past from a thin surviving record, not as proof that the missing deeds are thereby verified.

The comparison is precise but limited: Critias describes an ancient Athenian warrior class with communal property and says that it practiced the pursuits described yesterday for the hypothesized guardians. That links the two descriptions; it does not by itself establish that Socrates’ city once existed. The historical status of the ancient arrangement remains part of Critias’s account, not something certified by the comparison alone.

The passage’s force comes from layering kinds of evidence. Critias points to surviving roof-beams from mountains that now feed only bees, then shifts to a roof-tile image for soil that stores rain, and finally points to shrines at former springs as signs. I would hear this not as a demonstration that settles every detail of the ancient chronology, but as an invitation to let present traces make the vanished landscape imaginable.

Here the political portrait is made visible through domestic habits. The Athenians are said to use neither gold nor silver and to pursue a middle course between arrogance and illiberality; their orderly houses pass unchanged to later generations. The point, as I read it, is continuity: a civic way of life is pictured as something built into dwelling and inheritance, not merely announced as a principle.

The handoff places the enemy story in remembered speech: Critias says that he and his hearers heard it as children, then qualifies the offering with the possibility that memory may fail. I hear this not as a verdict on truth, but as a change in register: what follows is offered for communal possession, not simply asserted.

At the turning word τορνεύων, the passage lets us picture Poseidon's act through a craft gesture: the rings are not merely reported as present; they are imagined as shaped around the hill with deliberate circular precision. That image makes the island's geometry feel made and ordered. It would be too strong, however, to turn this single verb into a claim that the whole landscape is a worked artifact. The craft analogy sharpens the scene without settling everything about the terrain.

The aside about ships and sailing does more than explain why the rings block human access. By placing the scene in a time before either existed, Critias gives the island a temporal setting as well as a geography: this is a narrated past whose conditions differ from a later age of seafaring. The sentence thus helps the myth mark its distance from the narrator's present, without requiring any further claim about Atlantis's future.

revisions.title: From allotment to ordered building
revisions.body: This unit moves from ordered distribution of lands and titles to natural abundance, then to construction. Atlas is made king, succession follows the eldest line, and each son receives a territorial role. The catalogue presents fertility and animals before the narrative turns to an ordered building program: the first works described bridge the sea-rings and make a road toward the palace.

The naming sequence gives the imagined geography a genealogy. Atlas supplies the name of the island and sea; his twin is Eumelus in Greek but Gadeirus in the native tongue, and the Gadeiric region is linked to that name. Read this as the story’s naming device: it ties places to founders while marking a difference between languages. The passage itself does not establish a chain of Egyptian transmission into Greek.

The fertility catalogue does not simply end; it supplies the materials for the next movement. After naming the island’s produce and praising it as sacred, beautiful, wondrous, and boundless in quantity, the narration turns to what the inhabitants build. It begins with bridges across the sea-rings and a road toward the palace, then describes an ordered succession of adornment. Hear the shift from natural provision to deliberate arrangement.

revisions.title: From measured land to ordered power
revisions.body: This passage’s organizing move is to make Atlantis legible as an administered whole: measured terrain and engineered waterworks become territorial lots, military obligations, and finally a rule binding the ten kings. The levy is not uniformly fractional. Each leader contributes one sixth of a chariot, but the other listed forces are fixed numbers, alongside a fleet total of 1,200 ships. The final turn grounds inter-king relations in Poseidon’s written law.

revisions.title: When wealth changes meaning
revisions.body: At first, the rulers’ wealth is light because virtue governs its use; when the divine portion fades into mortal mixture, that abundance becomes a burden they cannot bear. The passage then reverses appearance and reality: those unable to perceive the truly happy life mistake lawless ambition and power for blessedness. Zeus sees the race’s wretched condition and gathers the gods, intending to chasten them.
